title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
directAnswer: All words have the SAME length L, so any valid concatenation is a block of L-sized chunks. Build a need-count map of the words. The brute force checks every start index by chopping the next k·L characters into words and matching counts (O(n·k) or O(n·k·L)). The optimal runs L sliding windows — one per alignment offset 0..L-1 — stepping by L word-by-word, maintaining a window count map and shrinking from the left on overflow, for O(n·L) time.

remember.pattern: Fixed-length sliding window stepping by word length + count map
remember.formula:
need = Counter(words); L = len(words[0]); k = len(words)
for offset in range(L):
    slide a window of words [left, right) stepping by L
    on each word: window[w]++ ; while window[w] > need[w]: drop left word
    if window holds k words: record left, then drop one to keep sliding
rules: Every word has the **same length L** — that's what makes a fixed-step window possible. Always state this first.
Run **L independent windows**, one per start offset `0..L-1`, so every possible word-aligned boundary is covered exactly once.
Step the window **by L (one word)**, never by 1 — the building block is a word, not a character.
On overflow (a word appears more than `need` allows, or an unknown word), **shrink/reset from the left** rather than restarting the scan.
Order within the concatenation **does not matter** and there must be **no gaps** — count equality of the k chunks is the whole condition.
whenToUse: Match a multiset of equal-length tokens as a contiguous block
All pattern pieces share one fixed length → window can step by that length
You'd otherwise re-scan overlapping windows and want to amortize with a sliding count map
antiSignals: Words have different lengths → can't step by a fixed L; needs a trie / DP word-break instead
Only one word or order matters → plain substring search (KMP)
Need the longest such window, not exact-length blocks → different window template
Tokens can overlap or repeat freely → not a fixed multiset match
remember.takeaway: The equal-length guarantee is the entire unlock: it turns a messy substring problem into 'slide a word-granular window and compare count maps'. The L-offset trick amortizes overlapping checks so each character is visited O(1) times per offset — O(n·L) overall, the hallmark of an interview-grade answer over the brute force.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit the fixed word length to reduce a daunting concatenation problem to a count-map comparison, and whether you can upgrade the brute force into an amortized sliding window across L alignment offsets.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-chopping and re-counting the full block at every single start index (correct but slow), or sliding by 1 character instead of by word length, or forgetting to shrink the window on overflow so counts drift.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with 'all words are the same length, so a valid match is k aligned chunks'. Give the brute force, then derive the L-offset sliding window and explain why each character is processed O(1) times per offset.

problemStatement:
You are given a string `s` and an array of strings `words`. All the strings of `words` are of the ***same length***.

A **concatenated substring** in `s` is a substring that contains all the strings of any permutation of `words` concatenated.

For example, if `words = ["ab", "cd", "ef"]`, then `"abcdef"`, `"abefcd"`, `"cdabef"`, `"cdefab"`, `"efabcd"`, and `"efcdab"` are all concatenated strings. `"acdbef"` is not because it is not the concatenation of any permutation.

Return the **starting indices** of all the concatenated substrings in `s`. You can return the answer in any order.
constraints: All words[i] are of the same length
s and words[i] consist of lowercase English letters
understanding: We need every index where the next k·L characters of s (k = number of words, L = each word's length) split cleanly into the multiset of `words` — each word used exactly as many times as it appears, in any order, with no characters in between. Because all words share length L, the substring is just k consecutive L-sized chunks, and the match condition is multiset (count) equality of those chunks against `words`.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are all words guaranteed to be the same length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the key property. It means a valid match is exactly k aligned chunks of length L, so I can step a window by L and compare count maps instead of doing general substring matching.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can words contain duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. So I use a count map (multiset), not a set — a word appearing twice in `words` must appear exactly twice in the window.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of words in the concatenation matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, any permutation counts. That's why count equality, not sequence equality, is the condition. There must be no gaps or extra characters between the words, though.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same starting index be reported once even if multiple permutations match there?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — each valid start index is reported once; permutations at the same index are the same substring window.

examples.explanation: At index 0: "barfoo" = bar+foo (a permutation). At index 9: "foobar" = foo+bar. Index 3 "foothe" fails (the not a word).
Two 'word's are required but the text never has two words plus good plus best contiguously; no start index works.
Index 6: foobarthe; 9: barthefoo; 12: thefoobar — each is a permutation of {bar, foo, the}.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Start Index
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first. It's clean and shows you reduced the problem to count-map comparison before optimizing.
hints: All words share length L and there are k of them, so any match occupies exactly k·L characters. How many start indices are even worth checking?
For each start i where i + k·L ≤ n, chop the block into k chunks of length L and tally them in a 'seen' map; compare against the 'need' map built from words.
Bail early: the moment a chunk isn't a needed word, or its seen-count exceeds its need-count, this start fails — move to i+1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are O(n) start indices; each does up to k substring-and-hash operations of length L → O(n·k·L), or O(n·k) if you treat substring hashing as O(1) amortized. The maps hold O(k) words of length L → O(k·L) space.
approaches.explanation:
Start by exploiting the one fact that tames the problem: **every word has the same length L**, and there are `k = words.length` of them, so any valid concatenation is exactly `k·L` characters long. That means only start indices `i` with `i + k·L ≤ n` can possibly match — and at each such `i`, the candidate substring is just `k` back-to-back chunks of length `L`.

**Reducing the match to count equality.** Build a `need` map once: `word → how many times it must appear`. For a given start `i`, walk the `k` chunks `s[i], s[i+L], s[i+2L], …`, tallying each into a fresh `seen` map. The substring matches **iff** `seen` equals `need` as multisets — order is irrelevant, only counts matter. Because we use counts rather than a set, duplicate words in `words` are handled correctly (a word needed twice must be seen twice).

**Why early termination keeps it practical.** We don't have to build the whole `seen` map before deciding. As we extract each chunk we check two things: (1) is the chunk even a needed word? If not, this start is dead — break. (2) Has this word now been seen more times than `need` allows? If so, also dead — break. Either failure lets us abandon start `i` immediately and try `i+1`. On random text most starts die after one or two chunks, so the practical cost is far below the worst case.

**Why it's correct but not what they want.** Each of the `O(n)` start positions can, in the worst case, scan all `k` chunks, and extracting/hashing a length-`L` chunk costs up to `O(L)`. That's `O(n·k·L)`. The redundancy is obvious once you see it: adjacent start indices that are multiples of `L` apart re-examine the *same* chunks over and over. The optimal approach eliminates exactly that re-work by sliding a window instead of rebuilding `seen` from scratch — which is the natural next thing to propose.
approaches.insight: The equal-length property collapses a scary 'find all concatenations' problem into 'compare two multisets of fixed-size chunks'. Once you frame matching as count-map equality with early exit, the brute force is short and obviously correct — the perfect springboard for the sliding-window optimization.

steps.action: chunks bar, foo — both needed, counts match
chunk foo ok, next s[6:9]='the' not a word
chunks foo, bar — both needed, counts match

java.explanation: Build the required multiset of words once.
Extract the j-th chunk of fixed length L.
Chunk isn't a needed word → this start can't match, bail.
Too many of this word → overflow, bail early.
All k chunks matched the multiset → record the start index.

edgeCases.input: words with a duplicate, e.g. [foo, foo]
edgeCases.behavior: need[foo]=2; a window with only one foo fails the count, two foos matches.

pitfalls: Using a set instead of a count map — breaks when words has duplicates.
Comparing sequence equality instead of multiset equality — order shouldn't matter.
Forgetting the early break, doing full O(k) work even on hopeless starts.

approaches.name: Sliding Window over L Offsets (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The interview answer. Explain the L alignment offsets and why each char is touched O(1) times per offset.
hints: The brute force re-examines the same chunks for many start indices. Adjacent valid starts differ by L, so group starts by their alignment: offset 0, 1, …, L-1.

For a fixed offset, the string is a sequence of words at positions offset, offset+L, offset+2L, …. Slide a window over THAT sequence, keeping a running count map and a count of how many words are in the window.
Expand right by one word each step. If a word over-fills (count > need) shrink from the left until it's valid. When the window holds exactly k words, record left, then drop one word to keep sliding.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the L offsets scans s once in steps of L; across an offset every word position is added once and removed at most once → O(n/L) word ops per offset, each O(L) for substring/hash, times L offsets ≈ O(n·L). Maps hold O(k) words → O(k·L) space.
approaches.explanation:
The brute force's waste is that start indices that are multiples of `L` apart re-chop the very same words. The sliding window removes that waste by processing each **alignment offset** as one continuous left-to-right sweep, reusing work between consecutive starts.

**Why L separate windows.** A valid match always begins at some index `i`, and within that match the word boundaries fall at `i, i+L, i+2L, …`. Two starts share their chunk boundaries exactly when they are congruent modulo `L`. So we partition all possible starts into `L` classes by `start mod L`. For each offset `0 ≤ offset < L`, the substring `s` viewed from that offset is a clean sequence of consecutive words, and a single sliding window over that sequence discovers every match in that class. Doing all `L` offsets covers every possible start with no overlap and no omission.

**The window mechanics.** Within one offset we keep `left` (the window's start), a `window` count map of the words currently inside, and `count` (how many words are in the window). We advance `right` by `L` each step, reading the next word `w`:

- If `w` is **not** a needed word, the whole window is invalidated — clear the map, reset `count = 0`, and jump `left` past `w`. Nothing ending at or before `w` can be part of a match, so we skip cleanly.
- If `w` **is** needed, add it to the window and increment `count`. Now it may be over-represented: **while** `window[w] > need[w]`, drop the leftmost word (`window[leftWord]--`, `left += L`, `count--`). This shrink restores the invariant that no word exceeds its required count, discarding the earliest copies that caused the overflow.
- When `count == k`, the window holds exactly the required multiset — record `left` as a match. Then slide forward by dropping the leftmost word so the search continues for the next window.

**Why each character is processed O(1) times per offset.** Across a single offset sweep, `right` moves forward monotonically and `left` only ever moves forward too. Every word position is **added to the window once** (when `right` passes it) and **removed at most once** (when `left` passes it). So the total add/remove work per offset is linear in the number of word positions, `O(n/L)`. Multiplying by the `O(L)` cost to slice and hash each length-`L` word, and summing over `L` offsets, gives `O(n·L)` — a clear win over the brute force's `O(n·k·L)` whenever `k` is large.

**Why shrinking beats restarting.** The naive fix on overflow would be to restart scanning from `left+L`, re-counting everything. Instead, decrementing the leftmost word and nudging `left` forward keeps all the still-valid counts intact — this *amortization* is the entire reason the window is faster than brute force. It's the same shrink-on-violation discipline as Minimum Window Substring and Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, just operating on word-sized units instead of characters.
approaches.insight: Group start indices by `start mod L` so each alignment becomes one linear sweep, then amortize overlapping checks by shrinking the window instead of rebuilding it. The fixed word length is what makes 'one window per offset' both necessary (alignments don't mix) and sufficient (L of them cover everything).

not needed → clear window, count=0, left=9

code.python:
from collections import Counter

def findSubstring(self, s: str, words: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    if not words:
        return []
    L = len(words[0])
    k = len(words)
    total = k * L
    res: list[int] = []
    if len(s) < total:
        return res
    need = Counter(words)
    for offset in range(L):
        left = offset
        count = 0
        window: dict[str, int] = {}
        right = offset
        while right + L <= len(s):
            word = s[right:right + L]
            if word in need:
                window[word] = window.get(word, 0) + 1
                count += 1
                while window[word] > need[word]:
                    left_word = s[left:left + L]
                    window[left_word] -= 1
                    left += L
                    count -= 1
                if count == k:
                    res.append(left)
                    left_word = s[left:left + L]
                    window[left_word] -= 1
                    left += L
                    count -= 1
            else:
                window.clear()
                count = 0
                left = right + L
            right += L
    return res

java.explanation: One window per alignment class — covers every word-aligned start exactly once.

java.line: for (int right = offset; right + L <= s.length(); right += L) {
java.explanation: Step by L: the unit of movement is a whole word.
Overflow of this word → shrink from the left until the invariant holds.
Window holds the full multiset → record left, then drop one word to keep sliding.

java.line: } else { window.clear(); count = 0; left = right + L; }
java.explanation: Unknown word breaks any window through here — reset past it.

python.explanation: Process each of the L alignments as an independent sweep.
Shrink from the left to remove the excess copies of this word.
Exactly k words and no overflow → left is a valid start; record it.

python.line: else: window.clear(); count = 0; left = right + L
python.explanation: A non-word resets the window past itself.

diagrams.title: Window shrink on overflow
diagrams.caption: When a word over-fills, drop leftmost words by L until counts are valid again — amortized, not restarted.

edgeCases.behavior: need={foo:2}; window grows to two foos, count=2=k → record 0. No overflow because need allows 2.

edgeCases.input: repeated word forcing shrink, e.g. words=[bar,foo,foo], s="...foofoofoo..."
edgeCases.behavior: Third foo overflows need[foo]=2 → shrink drops the leftmost foo, sliding the window forward.

edgeCases.input: s exactly k·L long and matching
edgeCases.behavior: Single window per offset; offset that aligns records index 0.

pitfalls: Sliding by 1 character instead of L — re-introduces the brute-force redundancy and miscounts chunks.
Only running offset 0 — misses matches that start at non-multiples of L.
On overflow, restarting the scan from left+L instead of decrementing counts — loses the amortization.
Forgetting to drop one word after recording a match — the window never advances past a found start.

commonMistakes: Sliding the window by 1 character instead of by the word length L.
Using a set instead of a count map, breaking on duplicate words.
Running only one offset instead of all L alignment offsets.
On overflow, rebuilding the window from scratch instead of shrinking from the left.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stepping by 1 instead of by word length
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Words are length L, so chunk boundaries only make sense at multiples of L from the start. Stepping by 1 both re-creates brute-force redundancy and slices words at the wrong offsets.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Set instead of count map for duplicates
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If words = [foo, foo], a set loses the multiplicity and a window with a single foo would wrongly satisfy membership. Use counts.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
Set<String> need = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList(words));
// later: if (need.contains(word)) ...
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
Map<String,Integer> need = new HashMap<>();
for (String w : words) need.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not shrinking on overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When a word exceeds its needed count, restarting the scan loses the amortized cost guarantee. Decrement the leftmost word and advance left instead.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if window[word] > need[word]:
    window.clear(); count = 0; left = right  # over-resets, O(n*k)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while window[word] > need[word]:
    lw = s[left:left + L]
    window[lw] -= 1
    left += L
    count -= 1

patternNote: Fixed-length sliding window stepping by word length, run once per alignment offset, with a count-map multiset comparison. Recognise it whenever you must match a multiset of equal-length tokens as a contiguous block. The equal-length guarantee enables the word-granular step; the L-offset partition plus shrink-on-overflow is what amortizes it down to O(n·L). Cousin to Minimum Window Substring and Find All Anagrams.
